vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: To stop working, usually because you are older
A person who is still alive after a serious illness or a very bad event
A prize that you get because you did something very well
The same date as an important event in an earlier year
To think about things that happened in the past
An experienced person who helps a newer person at work
Working very hard for something because it is important to you

paras: This month, the Oncology Network celebrates its fifteenth anniversary. In 2011, it was a small team with one floor and twelve beds. Today it has four units, more than two hundred professionals and a lot of partners in Brazil and abroad. For this special edition, we talked to three people who have been part of the story.

Marta Lopes is a patient navigator. She has worked in the network since the first day, so for fifteen years. "I have helped more than three thousand families," she says. "When I look back, I remember every face." Many young nurses call her their mentor, and this year she will get the network's award for patient care.

Jorge Matos is a cancer survivor. He was a patient here in 2016, and he has been cancer-free since then. He has been a volunteer for six years. "Marta was my mentor," he says. "I have known her for ten years, and she is the most dedicated person in this building."

Dr. Paulo Reis has worked at the hospital since 2001, for more than two decades. He will retire next year. "Medicine has changed a lot since my first year," he says. "But the most important thing is the same: the team." And the network's business manager, Fernando Varela, has worked at Einstein for twenty-four years. His message for the anniversary is short: "We couldn't do it without our people."
reading.source: A short story written for this lesson, based on the Oncology Network where Fernando works.

listenings.text: Good evening, everyone. My name is Jorge Matos, and I am a cancer survivor. Ten years ago, I was a patient on the fourth floor of this hospital. I have been cancer-free since 2016, and I have been a volunteer here for six years. Every Tuesday, I sit with patients who are starting their treatment. I tell them my story, and I listen to theirs. My mentor here was Marta, the patient navigator. I have known her for ten years, and she has never stopped helping people. Tonight, the network celebrates its fifteenth anniversary, and I want to say one thing: thank you for my second life.

Hi Fernando, it's Sarah. I just read the anniversary newsletter. Congratulations! Fifteen years is a long time. And I didn't know this: you have worked at Einstein for twenty-four years! That's amazing. Our program in Texas is younger. We have had the family apartments since 2019, so only for seven years. I have a question for you, too. How long has Marta worked with patients? I want to invite her to speak at our conference in May. She is exactly the kind of mentor that our new nurses need. Call me when you can. Bye!
